captions.instagram:
How do landslides happen?

A hillside is a tug of war that gravity never stops pulling. Friction and cohesion hold the soil, until rain fills the ground, takes the friction away and the slope lets go. Tilt a slope until it fails, pour a sandpile, soak a hill in a cloudburst, switch road cuts, forests and drains on and off, and learn the signs that mean move now.

→ A hillside is a tug of war. Gravity pulls the soil down the slope. Friction and cohesion hold it.
→ Grip divided by pull is the factor of safety. Steepen the slope and it falls below 1: the soil lets go.
→ Pour dry sand and it settles at about 34 degrees: its angle of repose.
→ Rain fills the gaps between the grains. The water pushes back, the grains press less, and friction falls.
→ A cloudburst does in hours what a monsoon spell does in days. Below a factor of safety of 1, the slope goes.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/landslideclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How do landslides happen? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
A hillside is a tug of war that gravity never stops pulling. Friction and cohesion hold the soil, until rain fills the ground, takes the friction away and the slope lets go. Tilt a slope until it fails, pour a sandpile, soak a hill in a cloudburst, switch road cuts, forests and drains on and off, and learn the signs that mean move now.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/landslideclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/landslideclear

In this video:
• A slope in balance. A block of soil on a slope is pulled downhill by part of its weight and held by friction and cohesion.
• The angle of repose. Pour dry sand and it settles at about 34°, however big the pile.
• What rain does. Rain fills the gaps between soil grains, and the water pressure there carries part of the load.
• Kinds of landslide. Rock falls at tens of metres a second.
• What tips the balance. Slopes lose safety a piece at a time.
• India's slopes and staying safe. About 12.6% of India's land outside the snow, 0.42 million km², is landslide-prone: the Himalaya, the North-East and the Western Ghats.
